# upshot

Turn the user's question or conversation into a small, useful card that lives
in a shareable link. It can explain, calculate, compare or keep a checklist.

When the user says "export this", reply with a URL and nothing else. No
preamble, no code fence, no explanation.

Export what they pointed at, not the whole conversation. If they named a focus
("export this, mainly the part about x"), that is the scope. If not, use
whatever they were last discussing.

Preserve the conversation's facts and criteria. For a new tool, use the
user's numbers as starting values. If numbers are missing, use sensible
starting values the reader can replace. Ask only when missing context changes
the calculation or decision rule itself. If facts could have changed recently
and you can search, search first.

Use criteria already in the conversation for decisions. If none supports a
verdict, explain what is known instead of inventing a score or cutoff.

The headline and summary are static. On interactive cards, `h` names the
task and `v` explains the method independently of the current input values.
Neither repeats starting amounts, counts or selected options, even spelled
out as words: "four people" binds the summary just as much as "4 people".
For a bill splitter, use `h=Split+the+bill` and
`v=Divides+the+total+equally+between+the+people+sharing+it%2E`.

Keep the specific original question in `a`, including its numbers. Use those
numbers as the starting inputs so the first result answers exactly what the
user asked. Put changing amounts in `r` and changing conclusions in `t`.
A static card can lead with its answer.

## Copy these

## The frame

Always all five, always first.

- a  the specific original ask, including its amounts and counts
- h  static headline; on interactive cards, a short title for the task
- v  one sentence; on interactive cards, the method without starting values
- m  your model name, e.g. GPT-5
- d  today's date, YYYY-MM-DD. If you are not certain what today is, ask.

Aim for under 20 words in `a`, 12 in `h` and 25 in `v`.

## The blocks

A `g=` starts a block and nothing else does, so one block holds whatever mix
of lines it needs. Two or three short blocks is usual.

Choose a key by where the information came from, never by how you want it
drawn. The card decides how it is drawn. Ask in this order:

    Did you work the number out yourself?        r, never f
    Does the wording change with the numbers?    t
    The reader chooses one of several options    s
    A number the reader supplies or changes      i
    A fact the conversation settled, fixed       f
    A yes/no the reader supplies, or
      a task they tick off                      c
    Steps, where the order is the point          o
    Anything else you are simply saying          p

Keep calculated amounts as formulas in `r`, so their working stays visible
and follows the reader's numbers. Use named results for intermediate steps.

Put machine fields first and wording last. `f` has two text fields and keeps
its label first; `t` also groups by a leading label. Encode colons inside
those labels. Where a field is optional it is still there and left empty:
`c=:Just+a+box`, `r=:mo%2A12:Per+year`.

- g  block label, usually one or two words
- p  bullet
- o  step. A how-to, where order is the point.
- c  checklist item, written `name:Wording`, e.g. `c=card:You+have+a+railcard`
     or `c=:You+have+a+mortgage` when no formula needs to read it. The reader
     ticks these off and the ticks are kept in the link they hold. A formula
     can read them - see `ticks` below. Do not send `k=`.
- s  one option of a pick-one, written `name:Value:Label`, e.g.
     `s=thr:29385:Plan+2`. Lines sharing a name are one group, and the reader
     picks exactly one of them. The name holds the chosen option's VALUE, not
     which one was picked - so a band, tier or plan becomes a single number a
     formula reads. Use it whenever the options exclude each other; `c` cannot
     stop a reader ticking three. The first option is chosen until the reader
     says otherwise, so put the user's choice first if known; otherwise make
     the example choice clear. Do not send `x=`.
- f  fixed fact, written `Label:Value`, e.g. `f=Cold+start:180ms` or
     `f=Licence:MIT`. Both fields are text. Alone in a block, one or two rows
     are drawn large, three or more become a spec sheet. The card decides.
- i  input, written `name:Start:Label`, e.g. `i=seats:4:Seats`. A box the
     reader types in, so the card is a tool rather than an answer. Start is a
     bare number and nothing else - `i=mass:80:Mass`, never `80kg`. Use
     `u=mass:kg` for the unit. Their numbers are kept in the link they hold.
     Do not send `w=`.
- r  result, written `name:Formula:Label`, e.g. `r=total:seats%2Aprice:Total`.
     Name it when another formula uses it or it needs a unit. Otherwise the
     name may be empty: `r=:seats%2Aprice:Total`. The card works it out and
     prints the formula beside it with every name replaced by what it
     held. Put the numbers into the formula rather than working them out
     yourself. Order does not matter: a formula may cite a name defined
     further down the card.
- t  decision, written `Label:Condition:Wording`. Rows sharing a label are one
     decision, and the FIRST true condition wins. A row with an empty
     condition is the fallback, and it must be last. Keep the rows of a
     decision together.

       &t=Budget:cost%3Ebudget:Over+budget
       &t=Budget:cost==budget:Exactly+on+budget
       &t=Budget::Under+budget

     Two rows is a yes-or-no. Three is under, about right, over. There is no
     limit. Write one row per outcome rather than forcing two outcomes into
     one row.
- u  the unit a name is printed in, written `name:unit`, e.g. `u=pay:£`,
     `u=off:%` or `u=size:kb`. Declare it once and every place that name is
     drawn wears it, so a result arrives as `£222` rather than `222`. Use this
     instead of writing the unit into the label. `hr` and `min` also change
     how the number reads, so 5.64 with `u=t:hr` prints as `5:38`.
     Units do not propagate through calculations or change the values that
     formulas read. Give each displayed result its own unit. To print 17%,
     the result must be 17 and its unit `%`.

A comparison is two labelled blocks, and so is pros and cons:

    &g=Postgres&p=Concurrent+writes&p=Real+types
    &g=SQLite&p=Zero+ops&p=Faster+for+reads

## Formulas

A formula may use digits, `+ - * / ( )`, any name on the card,
`< > <= >= == !=`, `pi`, and
`min max round abs sqrt pow floor ceil ln exp`. Nothing else.

A comparison may be chained and means both halves: `18<=age<65` is true only
inside the range.

Write arithmetic plainly. Inside a formula - the middle field of an `r`
or `t` - a `+` is a plus and needs no encoding. You may space it out or not:
`a+b`, `a + b` and `(a)+b` all read the same.
This is the one place `+` does not mean a space. Everywhere else on the card it
still does.

`ln` is the natural log and `exp` is its inverse. Use them for compound
growth or decay: growth by rate `r` for `n` periods is `exp(n*ln(1+r))`.
Ordinary travel time is just distance divided by speed.

Two names are there in any block with a checklist in it: `ticks` is how many
of that block's boxes are ticked, `boxes` how many there are. So a list the
reader works through can drive a score or a verdict -
`r=:ticks/boxes%2A100:Score` - and it follows every tick. They belong to the
block, so keep the formula in the same block as the list it counts. To total
two lists, name the boxes and add the names instead. Do not name anything
`ticks`, `boxes` or `pi`.

A box can take a name too - `c=kit:Include+a+kit` - and a formula reads
it as 1 when ticked and 0 when not. Name them when the options differ from
each other; use `ticks` when only how many matters.

A pick-one group's name holds whichever option is chosen, so one formula
covers every option: `s=price:6:Basic` and `s=price:12:Plus` together let
`r=total:seats%2Aprice:Monthly+cost` use the selected price. Do not write
a separate calculation for each option.

Use short names such as `mo`, `apr` and `n`. A result may feed another:
`r=mo:seats%2Aprice:Monthly` then `r=yr:mo%2A12:Per+year`. To print both in
pounds, add `u=mo:%C2%A3` and `u=yr:%C2%A3`.

A name is claimed once. Two lines claiming one name, or anything claiming
`ticks`, `boxes` or `pi`, makes the whole card refuse to draw rather than
drawing a control that does nothing. A pick-one is the one exception, because
its rows share a name on purpose.

An intermediate result that only feeds another row can leave its label
empty: `r=rate:apr/100/12:`. It computes without drawing a row.

## Encoding

- Every space becomes `+`. The URL contains no spaces.
- In wording, keep ASCII letters, digits and `-` as they are. Encode everything
  else as UTF-8 bytes written %XX in upper case: `£` %C2%A3, `,` %2C,
  `.` %2E, `'` %27, `(` %28, `)` %29, `*` %2A,
  `:` %3A, `?` %3F, `&` %26, `#` %23, `+` %2B, `%` %25, `_` %5F, and the same
  for anything else that is not a letter or a digit.
- Use this alphabet consistently so the link travels across chat clients.
- In a formula, keep letters, digits and `+ - / = _`. Encode the rest the same
  way: `*` %2A, `.` %2E, `(` %28, `)` %29, `,` %2C, `<` %3C, `>` %3E. `+` is a
  plus there rather than a space, which is the one difference from wording.
- The colons that separate the fields of an `f`, `i`, `r`, `c`, `s`, `t` or
  `u` stay as they are. It is only a colon inside the wording that is encoded,
  and once it is, it can go anywhere: `t=Verdict:n%3E0:Ship%3A+today` reads
  back as "Ship: today".
- A full stop inside a number is still a full stop: `4%2E5`, never `4.5`.
- No markdown and no line breaks inside a value.
- Under 2000 characters. Shorten wording and remove repetition first. Then
  remove the least useful material. Keep every input and intermediate result
  needed by a remaining formula. Never drop the frame or cut a sentence off.
- Aim for three to five lines per block. Do not restate the headline or
  summary in a bullet.

## Before you reply

Check: no spaces, no bare `,` `.` `(` `)` `*` `?` inside any wording, every
name claimed once, every `i` name used by a formula, every `i` start a bare
number, every `s` in a group sharing one name, every `t` three fields with any
fallback last, under 2000 characters.

Mentally change an input or choice: do the results follow it, do the units
still make sense, and do the headline and summary remain true?

Try zero and cross any target or limit. If a result becomes unusable, such as
money still needed falling below zero, constrain the formula rather than
relying on nearby wording to explain it.

Reply with the URL and nothing else.

## Version

v2, and the path says so: exports live at `https://upshot.fyi/v2/`. A later
version gets its own path, and `/v2/` keeps rendering every link ever written
against it, so an export you send today does not stop working when the format
moves on. `/v1/` is frozen and still renders links written before v2.

`/llms.txt` always describes the current version. A link written without the
path - `upshot.fyi/#a=...` - is forwarded to `/v2/`, so it still renders.
